column1: # topic: Chapter 3: Colonization and Conflict in the South

column2: Powhatan was the weroance who united the Chesapeake Algonquians into a powerful confederacy and tolerated the English to gain trade goods and weapons against Piedmont rivals.
The Powhatan Confederacy united about thirty Chesapeake villages and some twenty thousand people under Powhatan until English expansion shattered its power.
The Pamunkeys were Powhatan's own people, whose homeland was gradually covered by English tobacco fields as colonization spread.
Pocahontas was Powhatan's favorite daughter, whose marriage to John Rolfe sealed an alliance that briefly eased relations between the Powhatans and the English.
John Smith was a soldier of fortune who briefly imposed order at Jamestown, bullied Indians into supplying food, and wrote influential accounts of Virginia.
John Rolfe was the Jamestown colonist who developed a marketable Virginia tobacco, starting the boom that fed English land hunger and labor demand.
Opechancanough was Powhatan's brother and successor who led great attacks on the tobacco colonists, but English retaliation destroyed the confederacy's power.
The Virginia Company of London was the joint-stock company that founded Jamestown in hopes of profit and governed early Virginia until the king dissolved it.
Jamestown was England's first permanent American settlement, built on Powhatan land, where disease, hunger, and conflict with Indians nearly destroyed the colony.
The House of Burgesses was Virginia's elected assembly, which began the tradition of representative government in England's American colonies.
The Calverts were the Catholic proprietors of Maryland who controlled its land and government and granted religious freedom to all Christians.
Charles II was the English king restored to the throne who began a more consistent colonial policy demanding that colonies enrich England.
Nathaniel Bacon was a wealthy frontier planter who led a rebellion against Governor Berkeley's Indian policy and favoritism, attacking Indians and burning Jamestown.
William Berkeley was Virginia's royal governor whose defensive Indian policy and favors to a small circle of allies angered frontier farmers and provoked Bacon's Rebellion.
John Coode was a Protestant Maryland planter who led a revolt against Calvert proprietary rule, which led England to revoke the Calverts' charter for a time.
The gentry were the wealthy Chesapeake planters who dominated offices, courts, and churches and built their fortunes on enslaved labor.
The Royal African Company was the English company that held a monopoly on the English slave trade until competing merchants were allowed in.
Juan de Oñate was a wealthy Spanish colonizer who founded the colony of New Mexico and crushed Acoma Pueblo's resistance with notorious brutality.
Acoma Pueblo, now called Sky City, was a fortified mesa-top community whose resistance to Spanish demands brought a siege, mass killing, and enslavement that became a symbol of Spanish cruelty.
The Franciscans were Catholic missionaries who built missions in New Mexico and Florida to convert Indians and persuaded Spain to keep its costly northern colonies.
Santa Fe was the Spanish capital of New Mexico, where soldiers, settlers, and captives lived amid the Pueblo communities that bore colonial demands.
St. Augustine was Spain's lasting fortified settlement in Florida, maintained to protect Spanish treasure fleets from pirates and rival colonies.
Popé was a Tewa religious leader who organized the Pueblo Revolt, the most successful Indian uprising against European rule in North America.
The Florida mission Indians lived in Franciscan missions and allied with Spain until Carolina slave raids devastated their towns and destroyed Spain's inland buffer.
Barbados was England's rich Caribbean sugar colony, whose land shortage sent planters and their slave system to found South Carolina.
Charles Town, at the Ashley–Cooper confluence, was South Carolina's center, where traders organized the Indian slave trade and shipped out the colony's exports.
The Yamasees were South Carolina's Indian trading partners who, fearing enslavement and betrayal, turned on the colony in a war that nearly destroyed it.
The Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Cherokee confederacies traded and raided for the English and survived by playing rival empires against one another.
James Oglethorpe was the Georgia trustee who planned the colony as a refuge for the worthy poor, with small farms and no slavery.
Quebec, founded by Samuel de Champlain on the St. Lawrence River, became the first permanent French settlement in North America, and Montreal, upriver, became New France's fur-trading hub.
The Pokanokets were a Wampanoag people of southeastern New England whose sachem, Massasoit, allied with the Plymouth colonists after epidemics had badly weakened his people.
Isabel de Tolosa Cortés Moctezuma was Juan de Oñate's wife, the granddaughter of Hernán Cortés and great-granddaughter of the Aztec ruler Moctezuma.
Juan de Zaldívar was Oñate's nephew who seized sacred turkeys at Acoma Pueblo and insulted the Acoma men, who then killed him and his companions.
Vicente de Zaldívar led the punitive expedition against Acoma Pueblo that killed perhaps 800 people, and he later failed to domesticate bison in a cottonwood corral.
King Philip III of Spain kept New Mexico after Franciscans claimed they had baptized thousands of Indians there since 1598.
The Tewa-speaking Pueblos evacuated a village for Oñate's settlers, and Pueblo women built the region's first Catholic church during early cautious cooperation.
The Jesuits were occasional Catholic rivals of the Franciscans and established missions in present-day Arizona while Franciscans dominated New Mexico.
Pedro Menéndez defeated the French at Fort Caroline in the 1560s, temporarily securing Florida for Spain before Indians and privateers destroyed most posts.
The Utes, Apaches, and Navajos were mounted peoples whom Spaniards raided for captives and whose own raids deepened New Mexico's crisis of famine and disease.
Pedro García gave August 1680 testimony that the Pueblo Revolt arose because Spanish and religious labor demands exhausted Indians and forbade them to plant their own crops.
Don Pedro Nanboa testified in September 1680 that Pueblo resentment came from Spanish suppression of sorcerers, idols, ancient customs, and religious practices.
Juan of the Tegua Nation testified in 1681 that El Popé of San Juan was the chief mover of the revolt and had Nicolás Bua killed to prevent a warning.
Adam Smith was the eighteenth-century economist who gave mercantilism its name, the theory that guided European commercial expansion for about two hundred years.
James I was the English king who chartered the Virginia Company in 1606, claimed Powhatan as a subject, and dissolved the company in 1624.
Chesapeake Bay was the Atlantic inlet fed by more than one hundred rivers and streams where the Virginia Company planted its colony.
Oliver Cromwell led the English republic that followed Charles I's 1649 execution and became a military dictatorship before the monarchy returned in 1660.
Charles I was the English king whose conflict with Parliament led elites and radical Puritans to overthrow and execute him in 1649.
The Dutch probably brought the first Africans to Virginia by 1619, dominated the slave trade until the mid-eighteenth century, and taught Barbados planters sugar processing.

column1: Dahomey, Asante, and the Lunda Empire
column2: Dahomey, Asante, and the Lunda Empire were African states built partly on profits from the expanding Atlantic slave trade.

column1: Gorée, Banana Islands, Cape Coast, and Bight of Benin
column2: Gorée, the Banana Islands, Cape Coast, and the Bight of Benin were West African coastal sites where captives were held before the Middle Passage.
The Gold Coast was the center of the African slave trade, holding more than one hundred European forts and trading posts.
Idia was the mother and adviser of Benin's leader Esigie, portrayed on a sixteenth-century ivory pendant mask ringed by Portuguese merchant faces signifying slave-trade wealth.
Dutch Guiana was the South American colony whose example shows the especially harsh conditions that enslaved Africans faced on plantations.
Sir John Colleton, with William Berkeley, persuaded Charles II in 1663 to grant the Carolinas to a group of joint proprietors.
Sir Anthony Ashley Cooper, Earl of Shaftesbury, sponsored the English and Barbadian immigrants who founded the first permanent South Carolina settlement in 1669.
John Locke helped Shaftesbury write the Fundamental Constitutions of Carolina, providing a proprietary governor, a hereditary Council of Lords, and an elected Parliament.
Albemarle Sound was the North Carolina area that Virginia settlers already occupied before the 1663 Carolina grant.
Governor James Moore of Carolina attacked Spanish St. Augustine and the Florida missions in 1702 and returned with hundreds of Indian captives.
Bede was the English monk who supposedly left his fellow monks sugar and spices before his death in 735 CE, when sugar was a rare luxury.
About 30,000 British immigrants settled St. Kitts, Barbados, Nevis, Montserrat, and Antigua within forty years after 1604, first growing low-quality tobacco.
The James River watermen were enslaved Africans who worked as boatmen on Virginia's James River rather than as plantation field hands.
Savannah was the Georgia town where Ashkenazi and Sephardi Jews established a Jewish community under the trustees' rule.
The Caribbean islands stretched from the Lesser Antilles toward Puerto Rico, Hispaniola, Jamaica, and Cuba, where English settlement became permanent after 1604.
